ex01: Arrays are written between square brackets, with the items separated by commas.
Each fruit is a string, so it needs quotes.
An empty array is just the two brackets with nothing between them.
ex02: If a list has 5 items, what is the index of the last one? Use `length` to write it for any size.
ex03: Count the items to get the length.
Indexes start at 0: index 1 is the second item.
Reading an index where there is no item doesn't crash. It gives a special 'no value' value.
ex04: Each step is one method call on `playlist`. Check the lesson's table to pick the right method for each end.
pop() and shift() return the item they removed. Assign that result to the matching variable.
Don't declare `lastRemoved` or `firstRemoved` again: they already exist, just assign to them.
ex05: First find out whether the name is in the list, and where.
indexOf gives -1 when the item isn't there, so it can answer both questions at once.
Indexes start at 0, but guest numbers start at 1.
ex06: Start with a variable at 0 before the loop.
Inside the loop, add the current item to that variable.
Return the variable after the loop ends, not inside it.
ex07: Start a counter at 0 before the loop.
Inside the loop, compare each item with the target using ===.
Only increase the counter when they are equal.
ex08: Start with the first number as the biggest you've seen so far. Starting at 0 fails when every number is negative.
Visit every number and replace your 'biggest so far' when you find a bigger one.
ex09: Handle the special cases first: not an array, or an empty array.
An average is the sum divided by how many numbers there are.
Dividing by the length of an empty list gives NaN. That's why you return early.
ex10: Start with an empty array that will hold the result.
A number is even when the remainder of dividing it by 2 is 0.
push each even number into the result array, then return it.
ex11: `const result = scores` doesn't copy anything: both names point to the same array.
Make `result` a new array with the same items. The lesson shows two ways to copy an array.
ex12: Start with an empty array for the result.
A for loop can count down: start at the last index and stop after index 0.
Another way: visit the items in order and add each one to the start of the result.
ex13: Page 1 starts at index 0. Where does page 2 start, if each page has pageSize items?
The start of a page is (pageNumber - 1) times pageSize. The end is the start plus pageSize.
slice doesn't mind if the end goes past the length of the array.
ex14: Three steps: make it lowercase, break it into words, glue the words back together.
split(' ') breaks on spaces. join('-') glues with dashes.
String methods can be chained, one after the other.
ex15: Create a new array with square brackets, and spread both arrays inside it.
The order inside the brackets is the order of the result.
ex16: One way: copy the array, then remove the item from the copy with splice.
Another way: take the part before the index and the part after it with slice, and merge them.
splice changes the array it's called on, so never call it on the original.
ex17: `sameArray = original` doesn't create a new array. How many arrays exist in this code?
push(4) is called through `sameArray`, but which array receives it?
=== on arrays checks whether both sides are the very same array, not whether they look alike.
ex18: The outer loop visits each row. Each row is itself an array.
The inner loop visits each number of the current row.
Keep a single total, declared before both loops.
ex19: Build the result one item at a time, starting with an empty array.
Before adding an item to the result, check whether the result already has it.
includes and indexOf both work to check the result.
ex20: There are 8 ways to win: 3 rows, 3 columns and 2 diagonals.
A line is a win when its three cells are equal AND not empty.
A loop from 0 to 2 can check row i and column i at the same time. Then check the two diagonals separately.
